What Adaptation Achieves
•  Shifts cultural frames deliberately and effectively
•  Adapts behavior to bridge across cultural difference
•  Maintains a primary cultural identity while flexing
•  Operates from multiple frames with growing fluency
•  Cultural competence is a skill set applied intentionally
Your Developmental Horizon
Expand your sense of self to include the movement between cultural worldviews. Shift from "using" cultural frames as tools to experiencing them as part of who you are — a multicultural identity.

Tutorial 1 of 10  ·  Adaptation → Integration (DMIS)
Beyond the IDI
Integration as a DMIS Identity Orientation — Not an IDI Score
Why This Matters
The IDI measures five orientations ending at Adaptation. Integration is the sixth stage of Bennett's original DMIS framework. It is not an IDI-scored orientation because research found that Integration describes an identity experience, not a measurable step of increasing intercultural competence. This deck explores Integration as a post-IDI developmental concept for learners already operating at Adaptation.
Learner Goals
Explain why Integration is part of the DMIS but not the IDI, and what that distinction means
Describe Integration as a shift in cultural identity rather than a gain in intercultural skill
Understand that Integration is not necessarily "better" than Adaptation — it is a different experience of self
Developmental Activity
Framework Comparison: Review the 5-stage IDC and the 6-stage DMIS side by side. Write a short paragraph explaining the difference to a colleague who asks, "If I maxed out my IDI at Adaptation, what comes next?" Focus on why Integration is about identity, not performance.
Reflection Question
Does the idea of an orientation beyond Adaptation resonate with your experience? Have you ever felt that your intercultural competence was not just a skill set but part of who you are? What prompted that feeling?
Facilitator Note
Frame this module carefully. Integration is aspirational but also nuanced — Bennett himself notes it is not necessarily preferable to Adaptation. Avoid positioning it as a "level up." Instead, present it as a different kind of developmental experience that some learners may already be encountering.

2
Tutorial 2 of 10  ·  Adaptation → Integration (DMIS)
What Integration Looks Like
Living at the Margins of Cultures — and Central to None
Why This Matters
At Integration, one's experience of self expands to include the movement in and out of different cultural worldviews. People at Integration construe their identities at the margins of two or more cultures and central to none. This is not rootlessness — it is a fundamentally multicultural sense of self in which perspective-shifting and bridge-building become part of how one defines who one is.
Learner Goals
Describe the lived experience of Integration using Bennett's framework of cultural marginality
Identify characteristics that distinguish Integration from high-level Adaptation
Recognize Integration patterns in yourself or colleagues — especially those with multicultural life histories
Developmental Activity
Identity Mapping: Draw a diagram with "You" at the center. Around it, place the cultural communities that have shaped you — family of origin, professional culture, ethnic identity, geographic identity, and any others. For each, note: Am I at the center of this culture, at its margin, or moving between it and another? Where do you feel most "at home" — and is "home" one place or several?
Reflection Question
Bennett describes people at Integration as living "at the margins of two or more cultures and central to none." Does that description feel freeing, unsettling, or both? What does it mean for your sense of belonging?
Facilitator Note
Integration is the lived experience of many people from non-dominant cultural backgrounds, long-term expatriates, bicultural families, and "global nomads." Some learners will recognize themselves immediately. Others may find the concept abstract. Meet both where they are.

3
Tutorial 3 of 10  ·  Adaptation → Integration (DMIS)
Encapsulated Marginality
When Living Between Cultures Becomes Alienation
Why This Matters
Bennett identifies two forms of cultural marginality at Integration. Encapsulated marginality is being "caught" between cultures — not fully belonging to any cultural community. It manifests as alienation, identity confusion, or feeling perpetually misunderstood. It is especially common among non-dominant group members navigating between heritage and dominant cultures.
Learner Goals
Define encapsulated marginality and explain how it differs from constructive marginality
Identify situations in your own experience or your colleagues' where encapsulated marginality may be operating
Understand encapsulated marginality as a developmental challenge, not a personal failing
Developmental Activity
Marginality Inventory: Think of a time you felt "caught between" two cultural expectations — where both groups saw you as an outsider or a traitor. Write: (1) What were the two cultural frames? (2) What was the cost of not fully belonging to either? (3) Did you resolve it — and if so, how? If not, what kept it unresolved?
Reflection Question
Who in your professional world might be experiencing encapsulated marginality right now — feeling caught between their cultural community and the organizational culture? What would it look like to support them without asking them to choose sides?
Facilitator Note
Encapsulated marginality is a real and painful experience. It often affects staff from non-dominant backgrounds who have developed high intercultural sensitivity but feel alienated from their own cultural community as a result. Handle this topic with care — it is not theoretical for many learners.
5 / 13

4
Tutorial 4 of 10  ·  Adaptation → Integration (DMIS)
Constructive Marginality
When Cultural Marginality Becomes Identity and Strength
Why This Matters
Constructive marginality resolves the identity challenge of Integration. People experiencing it see themselves as multicultural beings who constantly choose the most appropriate cultural context for their behavior. They define their identity through perspective-shifting and bridge-building. Living at the edge of cultures may occasionally be stressful, but it is more often exhilarating and fulfilling.
Learner Goals
Define constructive marginality and explain how it resolves the identity tension of Integration
Describe what it means to define one's identity through perspective-shifting rather than through a single cultural center
Identify one area of your own life where you may already be experiencing constructive marginality
Developmental Activity
Constructive Marginality Self-Assessment: Rate yourself 1–5 on each: (1) I can move between cultural frames without feeling I am losing myself. (2) I define who I am partly through my ability to bridge across cultures. (3) I find living between cultures more energizing than depleting. (4) Others see me as a cultural bridge-builder. (5) I choose which cultural frame to operate from rather than defaulting to one. Review your pattern — where are you strongest, and where is growth needed?
Reflection Question
Bennett says constructive marginals "do not lose themselves" because they define their identities in terms of perspective-shifting and bridge-building. Is that a stable identity — or does it require constant maintenance? What sustains it?
Facilitator Note
Constructive marginality is aspirational but real. Many intercultural professionals, multicultural individuals, and bicultural staff members at DSD may already be living this experience. Name it, validate it, and help learners see it as a legitimate and powerful way of being — not a consolation prize for not having a "real" cultural home.

5
Tutorial 5 of 10  ·  Adaptation → Integration (DMIS)
Integration in the DSD Context
Multicultural Identity as a Resource for Equity-Centered Service
Why This Matters
In disability services, staff who experience Integration — through multicultural life histories, bicultural identities, or long careers bridging communities — are a vital organizational resource. Their ability to move fluidly between cultural frames strengthens service delivery and team culture. But only if the organization recognizes and supports that capacity rather than taking it for granted.
Learner Goals
Identify how Integration-level cultural identity can strengthen DSD service delivery and team practice
Recognize the organizational responsibility to support staff who experience cultural marginality
Connect Integration to the One DSD commitment to equity and culturally responsive practice
Developmental Activity
Organizational Leverage Audit: Think of one colleague or team member who naturally bridges across cultural frames in your workplace. How does the organization recognize that capacity? Is it part of their job description, or is it invisible labor? What would change if DSD intentionally supported and valued that bridge-building role?
Reflection Question
What would it look like if DSD treated multicultural identity not as a background characteristic but as a professional competency — something to be developed, supported, and compensated? What systems would need to change?
Facilitator Note
This module bridges individual development and organizational practice. People at Integration often carry invisible cultural labor — interpreting, mediating, and bridge-building without formal recognition. Naming this dynamic and connecting it to equity practice makes the module immediately actionable for DSD leaders.

6
Tutorial 6 of 10  ·  Adaptation → Integration (DMIS)
The Cultural Bridge-Builder Role
Operating as a Multicultural Connector Across Contexts
Why This Matters
People at constructive marginality naturally take the role of cultural bridge-builder — facilitating understanding across cultural divides. This role is powerful but demanding: it requires holding multiple frames simultaneously, translating between them without distortion, and maintaining one's own multicultural identity while serving others' developmental needs.
Learner Goals
Describe the cultural bridge-builder role and the specific skills it requires
Identify one professional context where you currently function as a cultural bridge-builder
Develop strategies for sustaining the bridge-builder role without exhaustion or identity erosion
Developmental Activity
Bridge-Builder Journal: For one week, note every time you find yourself mediating, translating, or facilitating between cultural frames at work. For each instance: (1) What cultural frames were you bridging? (2) Did anyone ask you to do this, or did you do it naturally? (3) How did it feel — energizing, neutral, or depleting? At the end of the week, review: Is this labor visible or invisible?
Reflection Question
If bridge-building is central to your identity, what happens when the bridge is not wanted — when one side or both resist connection? How do you sustain your sense of purpose when the role is unrecognized or actively opposed?
Facilitator Note
Many staff at Integration experience bridge-building as both a calling and a burden. This module should validate the role while also acknowledging its costs. Encourage organizational leaders to make bridge-building visible work — not just something that "naturally multicultural" staff are expected to do for free.

7
Tutorial 7 of 10  ·  Adaptation → Integration (DMIS)
Identity Stability at Integration
Grounding Yourself When No Single Culture Is Home
Why This Matters
One of the central challenges of Integration is identity stability. When your sense of self is defined through movement between cultural frames rather than through allegiance to one, the question "Who am I, really?" can become persistent and sometimes destabilizing. Developing grounding practices — sources of stability that are not culture-dependent — is essential for sustaining Integration over time.
Learner Goals
Identify the specific identity challenges that accompany Integration-level cultural marginality
Describe two grounding practices that help you maintain a stable sense of self across cultural contexts
Distinguish between healthy fluidity and destabilizing rootlessness in multicultural identity
Developmental Activity
Grounding Inventory: List 5 things that give you a sense of "self" regardless of which cultural context you are in. These might be values, relationships, practices, or commitments. For each: Is this culture-dependent or culture-transcendent? When you feel most unmoored, which one do you reach for first? This inventory becomes your personal grounding toolkit.
Reflection Question
Is it possible to be "at home" in the movement itself — to find stability not in a fixed cultural center but in the practice of shifting? What would that feel like on your best day? What about on your worst?
Facilitator Note
Identity stability is rarely addressed in intercultural training, but it is the central developmental task at Integration. Some learners will find this deeply personal. Create space for honest reflection. The goal is not to resolve the tension but to develop sustainable ways of living within it.

8
Tutorial 8 of 10  ·  Adaptation → Integration (DMIS)
Integration and Ethical Complexity
When Multiple Cultural Frames Produce Conflicting Values
Why This Matters
People at Integration regularly encounter ethical complexity that others do not — because they genuinely hold multiple cultural value systems, they may face situations where those systems conflict. What one cultural frame considers just, another may consider harmful. Navigating these conflicts without retreating to a single frame or dismissing the other is a core challenge of Integration.
Learner Goals
Describe a situation where holding multiple cultural value systems produced genuine ethical tension
Explain the difference between ethical relativism and the ethical complexity of Integration
Develop a personal framework for making ethical decisions when cultural values conflict
Developmental Activity
Ethical Tension Case Study: Think of a real professional situation where two cultural value systems you hold led to conflicting guidance. Write: (1) What were the two cultural values? (2) What did each suggest you should do? (3) What did you actually do — and from which cultural frame did you decide? (4) How did the "other" frame respond inside you?
Reflection Question
Is it possible to hold two contradictory cultural values as genuinely valid — not as abstract concepts but as lived commitments? What does integrity mean when your cultural frames disagree with each other?
Facilitator Note
This module surfaces one of the most intellectually and emotionally demanding aspects of Integration. Ethical complexity at this level is not a problem to solve — it is a condition to navigate. Resist the urge to provide neat frameworks. Instead, help learners develop tolerance for the ambiguity that is inherent in a genuinely multicultural identity.

9
Tutorial 9 of 10  ·  Adaptation → Integration (DMIS)
Building Your Developmental Plan
Sustaining Growth at the Edge of the DMIS Continuum
Why This Matters
Development at Integration is not about "leveling up" — there is no stage beyond it. Instead, it is about deepening, stabilizing, and sustaining the multicultural identity that Integration represents. A development plan at this level focuses on grounding practices, community building, ethical navigation, and intentional use of one's bridge-building capacity.
Learner Goals
Draft a personal development plan with at least two goals focused on sustaining and deepening Integration
Identify one practice community — people who share the Integration experience — for mutual support
Establish a reflection structure for ongoing ethical navigation and identity maintenance
Developmental Activity
Integration Development Plan: Complete each prompt — (1) The aspect of my multicultural identity I most want to strengthen is... (2) The grounding practice I will use when cultural marginality feels depleting is... (3) The bridge-building context where I want to have the most impact is... (4) My practice community for this work is... (5) I will revisit this plan on...
Reflection Question
What does "development" mean when there is no next stage? How do you stay a learner when the model says you have arrived — and your lived experience tells you there is always more to integrate?
Facilitator Note
Development plans at Integration should feel qualitatively different from those at earlier orientations. They are less about behavioral skill-building and more about identity maintenance, community, and meaning-making. Help learners see this plan as a living document, not a performance target.
11 / 13
11

10
Tutorial 10 of 10  ·  Adaptation → Integration (DMIS)
Living at Integration
An Ongoing Practice of Multicultural Being
Why This Matters
Integration is not a destination — it is a way of being. Bennett describes people at constructive marginality as "constantly choosing the most appropriate cultural context for their behavior." This module invites learners to reflect on the full arc from Denial through Integration, honor the journey, and commit to living as a multicultural person in a world that often demands singular allegiance.
Learner Goals
Reflect on the full DMIS developmental arc and locate yourself honestly within it
Articulate what Integration means for your identity, your work, and your relationships
Commit to one ongoing practice that sustains your multicultural identity and bridge-building capacity
Developmental Activity
Full-Arc Reflection: Write a 1-page letter to your past self — the version of you who first encountered the DMIS or IDI. What has changed in how you experience cultural difference? What has changed in how you experience yourself? What advice would you give that earlier version of you about the journey ahead?
Reflection Question
Bennett writes that people at Integration "experience difference as an essential and joyful aspect of all life." Is that your experience? What would it take to get there — or to stay there?
Facilitator Note
End the series with both celebration and honesty. The full DMIS arc — Denial, Defense, Minimization, Acceptance, Adaptation, Integration — is a profound developmental journey. Not everyone reaches Integration, and not everyone needs to. What matters is the commitment to growth. Close with an invitation, not a mandate.

Your Path Forward
From Adaptation to Integration — A Summary
01
Expand Self
Let cultural frames become part of who you are, not just tools you use.
02
Name Marginality
Recognize cultural marginality as a real experience and navigate it honestly.
03
Build Bridges
Use your multicultural identity as a resource for connection and equity.
04
Stay Grounded
Find stability in movement. Your identity is the practice of shifting.
05
Keep Growing
There is no final stage. Integration deepens through living, not arriving.
